ncert_questions.q: Can you list 10 recombinant proteins which are used in medical practice? Find out where they are used therapeutically.
ncert_questions.a:
Recombinant proteins made by expressing a cloned human or other gene in a host cell, and their use:

  1. Insulin (humulin): treatment of diabetes mellitus.
  2. Human growth hormone: treatment of dwarfism (growth hormone deficiency).
  3. Erythropoietin: treatment of anaemia, especially in kidney failure.
  4. Interferon-α: treatment of hepatitis B and C and some cancers.
  5. Factor VIII: treatment of haemophilia A.
  6. Factor IX: treatment of haemophilia B.
  7. Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA): dissolving blood clots after a heart attack or stroke.
  8. Hepatitis B surface antigen: the recombinant hepatitis B vaccine.
  9. Interleukin-2: treatment of some cancers, such as kidney cancer.
  10. DNase I: treatment of cystic fibrosis (thins the mucus).
  11. Streptokinase (recombinant form): clot buster in myocardial infarction.
  12. Adenosine deaminase (ADA): enzyme replacement therapy for ADA deficiency (SCID).

Any ten of these are accepted; insulin, growth hormone, interferon, erythropoietin, factor VIII and the hepatitis B vaccine are the ones the examiner most expects.

ncert_questions.q: Make a chart (with diagrammatic representation) showing a restriction enzyme, the substrate DNA on which it acts, the site at which it cuts DNA and the product it produces.
ncert_questions.a:
Restriction enzyme: EcoR I (from Escherichia coli strain RY 13).
Substrate: double-stranded DNA containing the recognition sequence.
Recognition site (palindrome):
5′-G A A T T C-3′
3′-C T T A A G-5′
Site of cut: between G and A on both strands, a little away from the centre of the palindrome:
5′-G↓A A T T C-3′
3′-C T T A A↑G-5′
Products: two fragments, each with a single-stranded 5′ overhang AATT, called sticky ends. Left fragment: top strand ends ...G-3′, bottom strand ends ...CTTAA-5′ (overhang AATT reading 5′→3′). Right fragment: top strand begins 5′-AATTC..., bottom strand begins 3′-G... The two AATT overhangs are complementary to each other and to any other EcoR I sticky end.

The chart should be drawn as a table with four columns (enzyme, substrate, cut site, product) and the DNA sequences written in each. Because the same sticky ends are produced wherever the enzyme cuts, fragments from two different DNA sources cut with EcoR I can be joined by DNA ligase, which is the basis of making recombinant DNA. The same layout can be repeated for Hind III (5′-A↓AGCTT-3′) and BamH I (5′-G↓GATCC-3′).

ncert_questions.q: From what you have learnt, can you tell whether enzymes are bigger or DNA is bigger in molecular size? How did you know?
ncert_questions.a:
DNA is far bigger than an enzyme. Enzymes are proteins, and even a large enzyme is made of a few hundred to a few thousand amino acids; a restriction enzyme such as EcoR I is a dimer of about 276 amino acids per subunit. A DNA molecule, on the other hand, is a polymer of millions of nucleotides: the single circular chromosome of E. coli has about 4.6 × 106 base pairs, and a single human chromosome carries tens to hundreds of millions of base pairs. Even a small plasmid like pBR322 has 4361 base pairs, and a gene of about 1000 base pairs, which codes for a protein of about 330 amino acids, is only a tiny fraction of the DNA it sits in.

We can tell this from the chapter itself: a restriction enzyme 'inspects' the length of a DNA molecule, moving along it until it finds its six-base-pair recognition sequence, and a single DNA molecule is cut by many enzyme molecules into many fragments. A molecule that travels along another and cuts it at many places must be much smaller than the molecule it travels on. Also, the DNA of a cell has to be tightly packaged with proteins to fit inside the nucleus (Chapter 5), which again shows how enormous the DNA is compared with the proteins.

ncert_questions.q: What would be the molar concentration of human DNA in a human cell? Consult your teacher.
ncert_questions.a:
Molar concentration = number of moles of the substance ÷ volume of the solution. A diploid human cell has 46 chromosomes, and each chromosome is one DNA molecule, so a cell contains 46 DNA molecules.

Number of moles of DNA = 46 ÷ (6.022 × 1023) ≈ 7.6 × 10−23 mol.

The volume of a typical human cell is of the order of 10−12 L (about 1 picolitre; a 10 μm cube is 10−15 m3 = 10−12 L).

Molar concentration ≈ 7.6 × 10−23 mol ÷ 10−12 L ≈ 7.6 × 10−11 M, that is, of the order of 10−10 mol L−1.

Check: 46 molecules in 1 pL is 4.6 × 1013 molecules per litre; dividing by Avogadro's number, 4.6 × 1013 ÷ 6.022 × 1023 ≈ 7.6 × 10−11 M. The value is extremely small, which is why molecular biologists amplify the DNA by PCR or clone it before they can work with it. (If the concentration of nucleotides rather than molecules is asked, the human diploid genome has about 6.6 × 109 base pairs, i.e. 1.3 × 1010 nucleotides, which gives about 2 × 10−2 M nucleotides in the same volume.)

ncert_questions.q: Do eukaryotic cells have restriction endonucleases? Justify your answer.
ncert_questions.a:
No, eukaryotic cells do not have restriction endonucleases. Restriction endonucleases are a defence system of bacteria (prokaryotes) against invading bacteriophage DNA: the enzyme cuts the phage DNA at its recognition sequences, restricting phage growth, while the bacterium protects its own DNA by methylating those sequences with a companion modification enzyme.

Eukaryotes do not need this system; they are not infected by bacteriophages, and their own DNA is protected in the nucleus and packaged with histones. Also, eukaryotic DNA contains a large number of palindromic sequences of the kind restriction enzymes recognise; if a eukaryotic cell made such enzymes, its own genome would be cut to pieces, and eukaryotic DNA is generally not methylated in a way that would protect it from every restriction enzyme. All the more than 900 known restriction enzymes have been isolated from over 230 strains of bacteria, and none from a eukaryote, which supports the answer.

ncert_questions.q: Besides better aeration and mixing properties, what other advantages do stirred tank bioreactors have over shake flasks?
ncert_questions.a:
A shake flask holds a small volume and is shaken on a platform; it gives little control over conditions. A stirred-tank bioreactor has these advantages in addition to better aeration and mixing:

  • Large volume: 100 to 1000 litres of culture can be processed, so appreciable quantities of product are obtained.
  • Temperature control: a cooling jacket and temperature probe keep the culture at its optimum.
  • pH control: acid and base inlets and a pH probe adjust pH automatically.
  • Controlled oxygen delivery: sterile air is bubbled in through a sparger at a set rate.
  • Foam control: a foam breaker prevents foam from blocking the exhaust and contaminating the culture.
  • Sampling ports: small volumes can be withdrawn periodically for monitoring without opening the vessel, keeping the culture aseptic.
  • Continuous operation: used medium can be drained while fresh medium is added, keeping cells in the log phase for higher yield.

Together these give a reproducible, sterile, monitored process suited to producing recombinant proteins at commercial scale.

ncert_questions.q: Collect 5 examples of palindromic DNA sequences by consulting your teacher. Better try to create a palindromic sequence by following base-pair rules.
ncert_questions.a:
A palindromic DNA sequence reads the same on both strands in the 5′→3′ direction. Five examples, each the recognition site of a restriction enzyme:

  1. 5′-GAATTC-3′ / 3′-CTTAAG-5′ (EcoR I)
  2. 5′-AAGCTT-3′ / 3′-TTCGAA-5′ (Hind III)
  3. 5′-GGATCC-3′ / 3′-CCTAGG-5′ (BamH I)
  4. 5′-GTCGAC-3′ / 3′-CAGCTG-5′ (Sal I)
  5. 5′-CTGCAG-3′ / 3′-GACGTC-5′ (Pst I)

Additional ones: 5′-CAGCTG-3′ (Pvu II), 5′-ATCGAT-3′ (Cla I), 5′-GTPyPuAC-3′ (Hind II, where Py = C or T and Pu = A or G).

Creating one. Write any sequence for the first half, say 5′-CGT. Its complement is 3′-GCA. For a palindrome the second half must be the complement of the first half read backwards, so the second half is ACG. The full top strand is 5′-CGTACG-3′; pair each base to get the bottom strand 3′-GCATGC-5′; read the bottom strand 5′→3′ and it is CGTACG, the same as the top. The rule: take any sequence, write its reverse complement, and append it.

ncert_questions.q: Can you recall meiosis and indicate at what stage a recombinant DNA is made?
ncert_questions.a:
In meiosis, recombinant DNA is formed naturally during prophase I, in the sub-stage pachytene, when crossing over takes place. Homologous chromosomes pair during zygotene to form bivalents held together by the synaptonemal complex; at pachytene, non-sister chromatids of the homologous chromosomes exchange segments at chiasmata, catalysed by the enzyme recombinase. The exchange of genetic material between the two homologues produces chromatids carrying a new combination of alleles, which is recombinant DNA in the natural sense. The chiasmata become visible at diplotene and the recombined chromosomes separate at anaphase I.

In the laboratory, recombinant DNA is made in a similar spirit but by design: a DNA fragment from one source is joined to a vector using restriction enzymes and DNA ligase. Both natural crossing over and laboratory recombination produce DNA molecules whose sequence combines genetic material from two different sources.

ncert_questions.q: Can you think and answer how a reporter enzyme can be used to monitor transformation of host cells by foreign DNA in addition to a selectable marker?
ncert_questions.a:
A reporter enzyme is an enzyme whose gene is placed in the vector so that its activity, and not merely the survival of the cell, tells us whether the foreign DNA has entered and, better still, whether it has been inserted at the cloning site. The standard reporter is β-galactosidase, coded by the lacZ gene.

The cloning site is placed within the coding sequence of lacZ. Cells are plated on a medium containing a chromogenic substrate (a colourless compound that the enzyme converts into a blue product). If the vector has no insert, lacZ is intact, β-galactosidase is made, and the colony turns blue. If the foreign DNA has been inserted within lacZ, the gene is broken (insertional inactivation), no enzyme is made, and the colony stays white. So the reporter enzyme distinguishes recombinants (white) from non-recombinants (blue) on a single plate, in one step, by colour.

The selectable marker (say ampR) is still needed to remove cells that took up no vector at all: the plate also contains ampicillin, so cells without a plasmid do not grow. The two work together: the selectable marker selects transformants, and the reporter enzyme reports which transformants are recombinants. Other reporter enzymes used in the same way are green fluorescent protein (GFP), which fluoresces, and β-glucuronidase (GUS) in plants, which gives a blue product.

ncert_questions.q: Describe briefly the following: (a) Origin of replication (b) Bioreactors (c) Downstream processing
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Origin of replication (ori): a specific DNA sequence in a vector (or chromosome) from which replication starts. Any piece of DNA linked to an ori can be made to replicate within the host cell. The ori also controls the copy number of the linked DNA, so a vector is chosen with an ori that gives the copy number wanted. Alien DNA without an ori is not copied and is lost from the host.

(b) Bioreactors: vessels in which large volumes (100 to 1000 litres) of culture are processed to convert raw materials biologically into specific products, enzymes and so on, using microbial, plant, animal or human cells. They provide optimum conditions of temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins and oxygen. The most common type is the stirred-tank bioreactor, cylindrical or curved-based, with a stirrer for mixing and oxygen distribution; in the sparged version air is bubbled in. A bioreactor has an agitator system, an oxygen delivery system, a foam control system, temperature and pH control systems and sampling ports for periodic withdrawal of culture.

(c) Downstream processing: the series of processes a product is put through after the biosynthetic stage before it can be marketed. It includes separation of the product from the culture and its purification; the product is then formulated with suitable preservatives, drug formulations undergo thorough clinical trials, and every product is subjected to strict quality control testing. The exact steps vary from product to product.

ncert_questions.q: Explain briefly: (a) PCR (b) Restriction enzymes and DNA (c) Chitinase
ncert_questions.a:
(a) PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): a technique for making multiple copies of a gene or DNA segment in vitro. It uses the template DNA, two sets of primers (short synthetic oligonucleotides complementary to the regions flanking the target), a thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus) and the four deoxynucleotides. Each cycle has three steps: denaturation of the double-stranded DNA by heat (about 94 °C), annealing of the primers to the separated strands at a lower temperature, and extension of the primers by Taq polymerase at about 72 °C. Repeating the cycle about 30 times amplifies the segment about a billion times. The thermostable enzyme is essential because it survives the repeated high-temperature denaturation.

(b) Restriction enzymes and DNA: restriction endonucleases are bacterial enzymes that cut DNA at specific positions. Each enzyme inspects a DNA molecule, binds to its specific recognition sequence, which is a palindrome (for EcoR I, 5′-GAATTC-3′), and cuts each strand in its sugar–phosphate backbone a little away from the centre of the palindrome, leaving single-stranded sticky ends. Since a given enzyme produces the same sticky ends on any DNA, fragments of vector and foreign DNA cut with the same enzyme can be joined by DNA ligase to make recombinant DNA. Restriction enzymes are therefore the 'molecular scissors' of genetic engineering. Exonucleases, by contrast, remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA.

(c) Chitinase: an enzyme that digests chitin, the polysaccharide of the fungal cell wall. In recombinant DNA technology it is used to break open fungal (including yeast) cells to release their DNA during the isolation of genetic material, just as lysozyme is used for bacteria and cellulase for plant cells.

ncert_questions.q: Discuss with your teacher and find out how to distinguish between (a) Plasmid DNA and Chromosomal DNA (b) RNA and DNA (c) Exonuclease and Endonuclease
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Plasmid DNA vs chromosomal DNA: plasmid DNA is a small, circular, extra-chromosomal DNA of bacteria that replicates autonomously with its own ori, may be present in many copies per cell (1–2 to 15–100 or more), carries a few non-essential genes such as antibiotic resistance, and can be transferred between cells; it is used as a cloning vector. Chromosomal DNA is the single large circular (in bacteria) or linear (in eukaryotes) genome, present in one copy per cell in bacteria, carries all the essential genes, and in eukaryotes is packaged with histones inside the nucleus.

(b) RNA vs DNA: RNA has the sugar ribose (with a 2′-OH) and the base uracil in place of thymine, is usually single-stranded, is less stable (the 2′-OH makes it reactive and easily degraded) and is found as mRNA, tRNA and rRNA; it is removed during DNA isolation by ribonuclease. DNA has deoxyribose (2′-H) and thymine, is double-stranded and helical, is chemically and structurally more stable, and is the genetic material; it is removed by deoxyribonuclease.

(c) Exonuclease vs endonuclease: an exonuclease removes nucleotides one at a time from the ends (5′ or 3′) of a DNA molecule; it does not need a specific sequence. An endonuclease cuts within the DNA molecule, and a restriction endonuclease does so only at a specific recognition sequence, producing fragments; endonucleases such as EcoR I are used in recombinant DNA technology.

pyq.q: DNA fragments separated on an agarose gel can be visualised after staining with
options: Acetocarmine and viewing in visible light
Ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation
Safranin followed by exposure to infrared radiation
Methylene blue followed by exposure to X-rays
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Separated DNA is stained with ethidium bromide and exposed to UV light; it then appears as bright orange coloured bands. Pure DNA cannot be seen in visible light.

pyq.q: To release the DNA from a fungal cell during the isolation of genetic material, the cell wall is digested with the enzyme
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The fungal cell wall is made of chitin, so chitinase is used. Lysozyme is for bacteria and cellulase for plant cells; protease removes proteins after lysis.

pyq.q: In pBR322, an alien DNA is to be inserted so that it inactivates the tetracycline-resistance gene. Which restriction site should be used?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Sal I (and BamH I) lie within tet<sup>R</sup>. Pst I and Pvu I lie within amp<sup>R</sup>, and Pvu II lies near rop.

pyq.q: The first restriction endonuclease, Hind II, was found to recognise a specific sequence of
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Hind II always cuts DNA at a particular point within a recognition sequence of six base pairs.

pyq.q: The thermostable DNA polymerase used in PCR is isolated from
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Taq polymerase from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus remains active during the high-temperature denaturation step of every cycle.

pyq.q: Which of the following is not a feature of plasmids?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Plasmids are double-stranded, circular, extra-chromosomal DNA that replicate independently of the chromosome.

pyq.q: During gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments
options: move towards the cathode, and larger fragments move farther
move towards the anode, and smaller fragments move farther
move towards the anode, and larger fragments move farther
do not move unless they are positively charged
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: DNA is negatively charged and migrates towards the anode; the agarose sieving effect lets smaller fragments move farther.

pyq.q: In the name of the restriction enzyme EcoR I, the letter 'R' stands for
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: E is from Escherichia, co from coli, R from strain RY 13, and the Roman numeral I gives the order of isolation from that strain.

pyq.q: The plant pathogen that naturally delivers T-DNA into dicot cells and has been converted into a cloning vector is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Agrobacterium tumefaciens transfers T-DNA from its Ti plasmid into plant cells; the disarmed Ti plasmid is used as a vector for plants.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): EcoR I produces sticky ends when it cuts DNA. Reason (R): EcoR I cuts the DNA a little away from the centre of its palindromic recognition sequence, between the same two bases (G and A) on the opposite strands.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because the cuts on the two strands are staggered, each fragment is left with a single-stranded AATT overhang; these overhangs are the sticky ends. R is the reason for A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Bacterial cells are treated with a specific concentration of calcium ions before transformation. Reason (R): DNA is a hydrophilic molecule and cannot pass through the cell membrane on its own.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because DNA is hydrophilic it cannot cross the membrane; treatment with a divalent cation such as calcium makes the cells competent by increasing the efficiency with which DNA enters through pores in the cell wall.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): DNA ligase joins the vector and the foreign DNA fragment. Reason (R): DNA ligase forms hydrogen bonds between the complementary bases of the sticky ends.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: DNA ligase does join the two DNAs, but by forming phosphodiester bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone. The hydrogen bonds between sticky ends form on their own by base pairing and only hold the ends together until ligase acts.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): An alien piece of DNA introduced into a host cell must be linked to an origin of replication. Reason (R): DNA that is not part of a chromosome or not linked to an ori cannot replicate in the host and is lost.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: A piece of DNA multiplies in a host only if it becomes part of the chromosome or is joined to a DNA carrying an ori; otherwise it is not copied and disappears. R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): In a continuous culture bioreactor, used medium is drained from one side while fresh medium is added from the other. Reason (R): This keeps the cells in their physiologically most active log phase and gives a higher yield.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The continuous system replaces spent medium with fresh medium so that the cells remain in the exponential phase; larger biomass and higher product yield follow. R is the reason for A.

pyq.q: Write the recognition sequence of the restriction endonuclease EcoR I and state how it cuts the DNA. What are palindromic sequences?
pyq.answer:
EcoR I recognises the sequence
5′-G A A T T C-3′
3′-C T T A A G-5′
It cuts each strand between G and A, a little away from the centre of the palindrome, producing single-stranded overhangs (sticky ends) of AATT on each fragment. (1 mark)

A palindromic sequence is a sequence of base pairs that reads the same on the two strands when the orientation of reading is kept the same, for example GAATTC read 5′→3′ on both strands. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Name the source of the thermostable DNA polymerase used in PCR. Why is a thermostable polymerase used?
pyq.answer:
Source: the bacterium Thermus aquaticus; the enzyme is called Taq polymerase. (1 mark)

Each PCR cycle begins with denaturation of the double-stranded DNA at a high temperature (about 94 °C). An ordinary DNA polymerase would be destroyed in this step and would have to be added afresh every cycle. Taq polymerase remains active during the high-temperature denaturation, so the reaction can run through repeated cycles automatically and amplify the DNA about a billion times. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Name two methods by which recombinant DNA can be directly introduced into a host cell without making the cell competent. Mention the type of host cell for each.
pyq.answer:
(i) Micro-injection: the recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell using a fine glass needle. (1 mark)

(ii) Biolistics (gene gun): plant cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with the DNA. (1 mark)

(A third, also accepted: disarmed pathogen vectors such as Agrobacterium, which infect the plant cell and transfer the recombinant DNA.)

pyq.q: State the role of 'ori' and 'restriction sites' in the cloning vector pBR322.
pyq.answer:
ori (origin of replication): the sequence from which replication of the plasmid starts; any alien DNA linked to it is replicated inside the host. It also controls the copy number of the linked DNA. (1 mark)

Restriction (cloning) sites: single recognition sites for restriction enzymes (EcoR I, BamH I, Sal I, Pst I, Pvu I and others) at which the vector is cut so that the alien DNA can be ligated in. Sites within a marker gene (BamH I or Sal I in tetR, Pst I or Pvu I in ampR) allow recombinants to be identified by insertional inactivation. (1 mark)

pyq.q: How is a bacterial cell made competent to take up recombinant DNA? Describe the temperature treatment that follows.
pyq.answer:
The bacterial cells are treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium (Ca2+), which increases the efficiency with which DNA enters the cell through pores in its cell wall. (1 mark)

The competent cells are incubated with the recombinant DNA on ice, then placed briefly at 42 °C (heat shock), and then put back on ice. The heat shock forces the DNA into the cells. (1 mark)

pyq.q: What is elution? Why is agarose used as the matrix in gel electrophoresis?
pyq.answer:
Elution is the process of cutting out a separated DNA band from the agarose gel and extracting the DNA fragment from the gel piece, so that the purified fragment can be used for constructing recombinant DNA. (1 mark)

Agarose, a natural polymer extracted from sea weeds, forms a porous gel that acts as a sieve: DNA fragments moving through it towards the anode are resolved by size, the smaller fragments moving farther. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Explain the convention followed in naming the restriction enzyme EcoR I. Draw the recognition site and show how the enzyme cuts the DNA.
pyq.answer:
Naming: the first letter comes from the genus and the next two from the species of the bacterium from which the enzyme was isolated; then the strain; then a Roman numeral for the order of isolation. So EcoR I: E = Escherichia, co = coli, R = strain RY 13, I = first enzyme isolated from that strain. (1½ marks)

Recognition site and cut:
5′-G↓A A T T C-3′
3′-C T T A A↑G-5′
The site is a palindrome. EcoR I cuts between G and A on both strands, a little away from the centre, leaving single-stranded 5′-AATT overhangs (sticky ends) that can pair with the complementary sticky ends of any other DNA cut by the same enzyme and be joined by DNA ligase. (1½ marks)

pyq.q: The enzyme β-galactosidase is considered a better selectable marker than antibiotic resistance genes in pBR322. Justify.
pyq.answer:
With antibiotic markers (say the insert at BamH I of tetR): transformants are selected on an ampicillin plate, and then the colonies have to be transferred to a tetracycline plate. Recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline; non-recombinants grow on both. The selection needs simultaneous plating on two plates with different antibiotics, which is cumbersome. (1½ marks)

With β-galactosidase (the lacZ gene): the cloning site lies within the coding sequence of the enzyme. Cells are plated once on a medium with a chromogenic substrate. If the plasmid has no insert, the enzyme is made and the colonies are blue; if the insert is present, β-galactosidase is inactivated (insertional inactivation) and the colonies are white. Recombinants are identified in one step, on one plate, simply by colour, with no second antibiotic plate. Hence it is the better selectable marker. (1½ marks)

pyq.q: Draw a labelled diagram of a sparged stirred-tank bioreactor and state the function of any two of its components.
pyq.answer:
Diagram: a cylindrical vessel with a curved base; a motor at the top driving a central shaft with impellers (stirrer); a sparger (air inlet) at the bottom releasing bubbles; a foam breaker near the surface; a cooling jacket around the vessel; pH and temperature probes; inlets for acid/base and nutrients; a sampling port on the side; an air exhaust at the top and a product outlet at the bottom. (2 marks for a labelled sketch)

Functions (any two): the stirrer (agitator system) mixes the contents evenly and distributes oxygen throughout the reactor; the sparger bubbles sterile air through the culture to supply oxygen; the foam breaker controls foam; the cooling jacket and probes maintain the optimum temperature and pH; the sampling port lets small volumes be withdrawn periodically to monitor the culture. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Describe the steps of isolation of DNA from a plant cell for use in recombinant DNA technology. Why are ribonuclease and protease added?
pyq.answer:
(i) The plant cell is broken open by treating it with cellulase, which digests the cellulose cell wall, so that the DNA is released along with RNA, proteins, polysaccharides and lipids. (1 mark)

(ii) Ribonuclease is added to remove RNA and protease to remove proteins, because DNA must be pure and free from other macromolecules before a restriction enzyme can cut it; RNA and proteins (including DNA-bound proteins and enzymes released from the cell) would contaminate the DNA and interfere with digestion. Other molecules are removed by appropriate treatments. (1 mark)

(iii) The purified DNA is precipitated by adding chilled ethanol; it appears as a collection of fine threads in the suspension and can be spooled out. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Why is Agrobacterium tumefaciens called a natural genetic engineer of plants? How has it been made useful as a cloning vector?
pyq.answer:
Agrobacterium tumefaciens is a pathogen of several dicot plants. It carries a tumour-inducing (Ti) plasmid, and during infection it delivers a piece of this plasmid, the T-DNA, into the plant cell, where it integrates into the plant genome. The T-DNA transforms normal plant cells into a tumour (crown gall) and directs the tumour cells to produce the chemicals the bacterium needs. Because it transfers genes into plant cells naturally, it is called a natural genetic engineer. (1½ marks)

Biotechnologists have disarmed the Ti plasmid: the tumour-causing genes are removed so that it no longer causes disease, but the T-DNA border sequences that direct transfer are kept. A gene of interest placed between these borders is delivered by the bacterium into plant cells and integrated into their DNA. This is how most transgenic dicot plants, such as Bt cotton lines, are made. (1½ marks)

pyq.q: State the principle of gel electrophoresis. How are the separated DNA fragments visualised and how is a fragment of interest recovered for use?
pyq.answer:
Principle: DNA fragments carry a negative charge, so in an electric field they move towards the anode through a matrix of agarose (a natural polymer from sea weeds). The gel acts as a sieve and the fragments separate (resolve) according to size: the smaller the fragment, the farther it moves. (1½ marks)

Visualisation: the gel is stained with ethidium bromide and exposed to UV radiation; the DNA appears as bright orange coloured bands. (½ mark)

Recovery: the band of interest is cut out of the gel and the DNA is extracted from the gel piece (elution). The purified fragment is then used to construct recombinant DNA by ligating it into a vector. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Describe the roles of heat, primers and the bacterium Thermus aquaticus in the process of PCR. Draw a diagram to show the steps of one cycle.
pyq.answer:
PCR (polymerase chain reaction) makes multiple copies of a DNA segment in vitro. Each cycle has three steps:

  1. Denaturation: the double-stranded template DNA is heated to about 94 °C. Heat breaks the hydrogen bonds and separates the two strands, each of which then serves as a template. This is the role of heat. (1 mark)
  2. Annealing: the temperature is lowered (about 50–65 °C) so that the two primers, small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to the sequences flanking the target on the two strands, base-pair to their sites. Primers provide the free 3′-OH from which DNA polymerase can start synthesis; polymerase cannot begin on a bare template. (1 mark)
  3. Extension: at about 72 °C the thermostable DNA polymerase extends each primer in the 5′→3′ direction using the deoxynucleotides in the mixture, producing two double-stranded copies. (1 mark)

Role of Thermus aquaticus: it is the source of the thermostable Taq DNA polymerase. Because the enzyme remains active during the high-temperature denaturation step, it does not have to be added fresh every cycle and the reaction can be repeated automatically about 30 times, amplifying the segment about a billion times. The amplified DNA can then be ligated into a vector for cloning. (1 mark)

Diagram: template DNA → strands separated by heat (denaturation) → two primers annealed at opposite ends on opposite strands → Taq polymerase extending each primer (extension) → two copies; arrow 'repeat' → four copies. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Draw a schematic diagram of the E. coli cloning vector pBR322 and mark the origin of replication, the genes for antibiotic resistance, rop and any four restriction sites. State the role of rop and explain how the antibiotic resistance genes act as selectable markers through insertional inactivation.
pyq.answer:
Diagram: a circle marked pBR322 with: ori at the lower left; ampR on the left arc containing the Pst I and Pvu I sites; tetR on the right arc containing the BamH I and Sal I sites; rop at the lower right with Pvu II near it; and Hind III, EcoR I and Cla I at the top. (2 marks)

rop: codes for the proteins involved in the replication of the plasmid. (½ mark)

Selectable markers: ampR and tetR confer resistance to ampicillin and tetracycline. Normal E. coli cells carry no resistance, so a cell that grows on an antibiotic must have received the plasmid; this helps identify and eliminate non-transformants and selectively allows transformants to grow. (1 mark)

Insertional inactivation: if the alien DNA is ligated at the BamH I (or Sal I) site of tetR, that gene is broken and the recombinant plasmid loses tetracycline resistance while keeping ampicillin resistance. The transformed cells are plated on ampicillin, where all cells carrying a plasmid grow; the colonies are then transferred to a tetracycline plate. Recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline, whereas non-recombinants grow on both. Thus one antibiotic selects transformants and the second distinguishes recombinants. (1½ marks)

pyq.q: (a) Why must a bacterial cell be made competent before transformation? Describe the method by which E. coli is made competent and transformed with recombinant DNA. (b) State the principle of gel electrophoresis and the role of ethidium bromide.
pyq.answer:
(a) DNA is a hydrophilic molecule and cannot pass through the cell membrane on its own, so the host must first be made competent, that is, able to take up DNA from its surroundings. (1 mark)
Method: the bacterial cells are treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium, which increases the efficiency with which DNA enters the cell through pores in the cell wall. The competent cells are incubated with the recombinant DNA on ice, then placed briefly at 42 °C (heat shock), and then returned to ice. The heat shock forces the DNA into the cells. Transformed cells are then identified by plating on a medium containing the antibiotic to which the vector carries resistance; only transformants grow. (2 marks)

(b) Principle: DNA fragments are negatively charged and move towards the anode through an agarose gel under an electric field; the gel provides a sieving effect so that the fragments separate according to size, the smaller fragments moving farther. (1½ marks)
Ethidium bromide: the separated DNA is invisible; the gel is stained with ethidium bromide and exposed to UV radiation, and the DNA is then seen as bright orange coloured bands, which can be cut out and eluted. (½ mark)

pyq.q: Describe the steps involved in recombinant DNA technology, from the isolation of DNA to the recovery of the product, naming the tool or enzyme used at each step.
pyq.answer:
1. Isolation of DNA: cells are opened with lysozyme (bacteria), cellulase (plant) or chitinase (fungus); RNA is removed with ribonuclease and proteins with protease; DNA is precipitated with chilled ethanol as fine threads. (1 mark)
  2. Cutting at specific sites: the purified DNA and the vector are digested with the same restriction endonuclease (e.g. EcoR I) under optimum conditions, giving fragments with matching sticky ends. The progress of digestion is checked, and the fragment of interest separated and eluted, by agarose gel electrophoresis. (1 mark)
  3. Amplification: if required, the gene of interest is amplified by PCR using two primers and Taq polymerase (from Thermus aquaticus) through cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. (½ mark)
  4. Ligation into the vector: the fragment is joined to the cut vector (e.g. pBR322, which has an ori, selectable markers and cloning sites) by DNA ligase, giving recombinant DNA. (½ mark)
  5. Insertion into the host: the host is made competent with calcium ions and heat shock (or DNA is delivered by micro-injection, gene gun or a disarmed Agrobacterium); transformants are selected on an antibiotic plate and recombinants identified by insertional inactivation or blue–white selection. (1 mark)
  6. Obtaining the product: the recombinant host is cultured on a large scale in a stirred-tank bioreactor under optimum temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrients, often as a continuous culture, so that the gene is expressed and the recombinant protein made. (½ mark)
  7. Downstream processing: the product is separated and purified, formulated with preservatives, put through clinical trials if it is a drug, and subjected to quality control. (½ mark)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A student is given the map of pBR322. She wants to clone a gene into the plasmid and pick out the bacterial colonies that carry the recombinant plasmid. She cuts both the gene and the plasmid with BamH I, ligates them, transforms competent E. coli cells, and spreads the cells on a plate containing ampicillin. Next day she transfers each colony to a fresh plate containing tetracycline.
(i) Why did she cut the gene and the plasmid with the same enzyme?
(ii) Which gene of pBR322 is inactivated by inserting at BamH I?
(iii) Which colonies on the tetracycline plate are the recombinants, and why?
(iv) Name an alternative marker that would let her identify recombinants on a single plate, and state how.
pyq.answer:
(i) Cutting both with BamH I gives the same sticky ends on the gene and on the opened plasmid, so the two can base-pair and be joined by DNA ligase. (1 mark)

(ii) BamH I lies within the tetracycline-resistance gene (tetR), which is inactivated by the insert (insertional inactivation). (1 mark)

(iii) The colonies that grew on ampicillin but fail to grow on tetracycline are the recombinants, because their tetR gene has been broken by the insert; non-recombinants, with an intact plasmid, grow on both plates. (1 mark)

(iv) β-galactosidase (the lacZ gene). If the cloning site lies within lacZ, then on a plate with a chromogenic substrate colonies without an insert are blue and colonies with the insert (recombinants) are white, so recombinants are identified by colour on one plate. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A forensic laboratory receives a tiny sample of DNA from a crime scene, far too little to analyse directly. The technician sets up a reaction containing the sample, two short synthetic oligonucleotides, a DNA polymerase from a bacterium that lives in hot springs, and the four deoxynucleotides, and runs 30 cycles in a thermal cycler in which the temperature goes to 94 °C, then to 55 °C, then to 72 °C in each cycle.
(i) Name the technique and the enzyme used, with its source.
(ii) What happens at 94 °C and why can the enzyme survive it?
(iii) What is the function of the two oligonucleotides, and at which temperature do they act?
(iv) Approximately how many copies of the DNA segment are obtained after the 30 cycles?
pyq.answer:
(i) Polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The enzyme is Taq DNA polymerase, a thermostable DNA polymerase from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus. (1 mark)

(ii) At 94 °C the double-stranded DNA is denatured: the hydrogen bonds break and the strands separate, each serving as a template. Taq polymerase is thermostable and remains active at this temperature, so it is not destroyed in each cycle. (1 mark)

(iii) The oligonucleotides are primers. They are complementary to the regions flanking the target segment, one on each strand, and they anneal to the separated strands at 55 °C; the polymerase then extends them at 72 °C. (1 mark)

(iv) The number of copies roughly doubles each cycle, 230 ≈ 109, so about a billion copies of the segment are made, enough to analyse. (1 mark)

practice_mcq.explanation: Pst I and Pvu I are inside the ampicillin-resistance gene; BamH I and Sal I are inside the tetracycline-resistance gene.

options: Proteins involved in replication of the plasmid

practice_mcq.explanation: The tumour-inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens delivers T-DNA into dicot plant cells; a disarmed version is the vector.

practice_mcq.explanation: Downstream processing begins after the biosynthetic stage and includes separation, purification, formulation with preservatives and quality control.

common_mistakes: Writing the EcoR I site without the 5′ and 3′ labels, or cutting it in the middle. The cut is between G and A on both strands, a little away from the centre, and the palindrome must be shown reading GAATTC 5′→3′ on both strands.

Saying DNA moves towards the cathode, or that larger fragments move farther. DNA is negatively charged and moves towards the anode, and the sieving effect of agarose lets the smaller fragments move farther.
Mixing up the pBR322 sites: Pst I and Pvu I are in amp<sup>R</sup>, BamH I and Sal I in tet<sup>R</sup>, Pvu II near rop. Also calling rop a selectable marker; it codes for replication proteins.
Reversing the two-plate result. Recombinants (insert in tet<sup>R</sup>) grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline; non-recombinants grow on both; cells with no plasmid grow on neither.

Swapping the cell-wall enzymes: lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plants, chitinase for fungi. And writing 'ethanol' without 'chilled', or forgetting that ribonuclease and protease remove RNA and protein.

Describing PCR without primers, or with the steps in the wrong order, or naming E. coli as the source of the polymerase. The enzyme is Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, and the order is denaturation, annealing, extension.
Calling ethidium bromide a 'dye seen in visible light' or saying the bands are green or blue. The stained gel is exposed to UV and the bands are bright orange.
Writing 'heat shock' without 42 °C or without the ice steps, and forgetting to say why competence is needed: DNA is hydrophilic and cannot cross the membrane.

Answering the bioreactor question with a diagram but no components, or listing fermentation as downstream processing. Downstream processing is separation, purification, formulation and quality control after the culture.
strategy:
This chapter is small in pages but large in marks per page, and almost every question is one of about ten set pieces. Prepare it as ten answers you can write from memory, each with its diagram: (1) the two core techniques and three steps of genetic modification, (2) EcoR I naming and the cut palindrome, (3) gel electrophoresis from principle to elution, (4) the pBR322 map with ori, ampR, tetR, rop and the sites, (5) insertional inactivation on two plates and blue–white selection on one, (6) Agrobacterium and retroviruses as disarmed vectors, (7) competent cells with calcium and 42 °C heat shock plus micro-injection and the gene gun, (8) DNA isolation with the three wall enzymes, ribonuclease, protease and chilled ethanol, (9) PCR with the three steps, primers and Taq, and (10) the sparged stirred-tank bioreactor with its six components, continuous culture and downstream processing.

Draw every diagram at least three times before the exam: the EcoR I cut, the pBR322 circle, the gel, the PCR cycle and the bioreactor. Boards reward a neat, fully labelled figure even when the prose is short. Write labels in NCERT's words.

For 1-mark items, make a fact card of numbers and names: 1963, Hind II and six base pairs, more than 900 enzymes from over 230 strains, 1972 Cohen and Boyer, 15–100 copies, 100–1000 litres, 42 °C, Thermus aquaticus, a billion copies. For 2-mark items, practise pairs: ori and cloning site, exonuclease and endonuclease, transformant and recombinant, micro-injection and biolistics.

Time allocation on the day: the 5-mark question from this unit is usually PCR, pBR322 or the bioreactor. Spend eight to nine minutes on it, with the diagram first, then the numbered points. Read Chapter 10 alongside this one; the paper often sets a case that begins with a technique from here and ends with an application from there.
revision_checklist: EFB definition of biotechnology and the two core techniques of modern biotechnology
Three basic steps of genetically modifying an organism; Cohen and Boyer, 1972, Salmonella typhimurium plasmid, DNA ligase
Five key tools: restriction enzymes, polymerases, ligases, vectors, host
Restriction enzymes: 1963 discovery, Hind II (six base pairs), > 900 enzymes from > 230 strains; exonuclease vs endonuclease
EcoR I naming (E, co, R, I) and the cut palindrome 5′-G↓AATTC-3′ with sticky ends
Gel electrophoresis: negative DNA to the anode, agarose from sea weeds, sieving effect, ethidium bromide + UV, bright orange bands, elution
Vector features: ori (replication start and copy number), selectable marker, single cloning sites; copy numbers 1–2 vs 15–100
pBR322 map: ori, amp<sup>R</sup> (Pst I, Pvu I), tet<sup>R</sup> (BamH I, Sal I), rop (Pvu II), Hind III, EcoR I, Cla I
Insertional inactivation: two-plate method with ampicillin then tetracycline; blue–white selection with β-galactosidase and a chromogenic substrate
Agrobacterium tumefaciens Ti plasmid and T-DNA; retroviruses; both used after disarming
Competent host: hydrophilic DNA, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, ice → 42 °C heat shock → ice; micro-injection (animal), gene gun with gold/tungsten (plant), disarmed pathogens
DNA isolation: lysozyme, cellulase, chitinase; ribonuclease, protease; chilled ethanol, fine threads
Cutting and ligation: same restriction enzyme for vector and insert, ligase makes phosphodiester bonds, check digestion on a gel
PCR: denaturation (≈94 °C), annealing (≈50–65 °C), extension (≈72 °C); two primers; Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus; ≈ a billion copies
Selectable marker in action: amp<sup>R</sup> rDNA into E. coli, plate on ampicillin, only transformants grow
Bioreactor: 100–1000 L, stirred-tank and sparged types, six components, continuous culture in the log phase
Downstream processing: separation, purification, formulation with preservatives, clinical trials, quality control; varies by product
